title: Multiplayer matchmaking
like: finding a match in an online game
brief: Players press Play and wait. You must put them in a match with others nearby, with similar skill, in a few seconds. Players in a far-away region will have a bad time, so you must keep each region close.

clarify.q: How long may a player wait?
clarify.a: Most should be matched within 10 seconds. Being matched slowly beats being matched badly far away.
Only when a region is empty or down. Normally keep them local: a ping above 80 ms feels bad.

clarify.q: Do we keep waiting tickets if a machine fails?
clarify.a: It is fine to lose waiting tickets. Players just press Play again.

notes: Each waiting player polls or holds a connection until matched (approx.).
Lobby messages are tiny, about 1 KB.

Lobby messages per second at peak
Open connections for waiting players
numbers.how: 3 million online ÷ 100,000 per gateway node ≈ 30 nodes (approx.)

hints: Where should a player be matched: near them or in one big pool in one place?
Run a stack in each region and send players to the nearest with geo-DNS. Lobby messages use a socket gateway.
Waiting time and match quality are an explicit policy tradeoff. Measure the failed boundary, waiting time and retry work before choosing a change.

editorial.summary: Keep matchmaking local. Each region has its own pool of waiting tickets, so players match with people close by. Geo-DNS sends each player to the nearest region and reroutes when a region fails.

designs.name: Three independent regions
designs.why: US, EU and APAC each run a complete stack. Tickets never cross an ocean, latency stays low, and a failure in one region does not affect the others.

tradeoffs: Waiting longer lets the matcher find a better skill match; matching instantly gives lopsided games.
Regional pools give low ping but small pools at night. You may widen the search over time.
Tickets in memory are fast but lost on a crash. Games accept that: the player simply queues again.
Geo-DNS with failover is what lets players still find a match when a region is down.
editorial.realWorld: A big online game can have millions of players online at peak, most idle in menus. Matchmaking aims for a ping under about 50 to 80 ms (approx.).

correctness.prompt: Multiplayer matchmaking: which invariant does this trace protect, and what failure would break it?
correctness.discussion: Claim players into one compatible match while widening search predictably. Duplicate entries can put one player into two matches. Roster publication must not precede exclusive ownership. Waiting time and match quality are an explicit policy tradeoff.

fields.label: Step 1. Player P retries Join after losing its reply. What queue entry exists?
options: One active entry keyed by player and matchmaking attempt
A fresh entry on every request
fields.explanation: Duplicate entries can put one player into two matches.

fields.label: Step 2. Two match builders select P simultaneously. What decides?
options: An atomic claim of all roster entries or a recoverable reservation protocol
fields.explanation: Roster publication must not precede exclusive ownership.

fields.label: Step 3. P waits beyond the target in a sparse region. What widens?
options: Merge all regions without a ping limit
A declared skill or latency bound over time, with a maximum acceptable ping
fields.explanation: Waiting time and match quality are an explicit policy tradeoff.

correctness.responsibility: Claim players into one compatible match while widening search predictably.
correctness.limits: The traffic model does not execute this protocol. The checked trace covers its central responsibility; the written explanation is retained for review.
